title: Patent Litigation Part Six: An Introduction to Patent Claims, "Limitations," Infringement, and Invalidity (DisputeSoft)

extracted.subtask_description: Introduces claim limitations as the unit of comparison for both infringement and invalidity, the three-step limitation-by-limitation analysis (identify, map, explain), claim chart structure and requirements, and the "aping the claim language" failure pattern for spotting weak mappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation independent of terminology — functional element matters
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation represents a single, scope-defining component within a broader claim structure. A limitation need not use identical terminology to what appears in the accused product — different naming conventions do not prevent infringement if the functional elements match.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same principle governs whether prior art discloses a limitation for invalidity purposes: what matters is the underlying element, not the label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction precedes any claim-to-reference comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Before comparing any claim to an accused product or prior-art reference, claim construction must occur, drawing from the claim language itself, the patent specification, patent drawings, the prosecution history, and relevant technical dictionaries and industry standards. This construction phase typically culminates in a "Markman hearing," where a judge determines the proper meaning of disputed claim terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-step limitation-by-limitation infringement analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Identify Every Limitation — divide the claim into individual limitations (semicolons often mark boundaries, but only as a starting point). Step 2: Map Each Limitation to the Accused Product (or Reference) — identify a corresponding feature, component, or step, specific to where and how it exists. Step 3: Explain the Correspondence — simply juxtaposing claim language with product/reference features proves insufficient; the analysis must explain how the feature satisfies the claim limitation's requirements and what functional or structural equivalence exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim chart four requirements: comprehensiveness, location, mechanism, contention
rubrics_metrics.description: Charts must include "specifically where and how each limitation of each asserted claim is found within each Accused Instrumentality." This imposes four distinct requirements: (1) Comprehensiveness — every asserted claim, every limitation, every accused product must be charted (representative products may substitute for closely related variants if representativeness can be justified); (2) Specificity of Location — part names, component designations, source code filenames, or functional locations; (3) Specificity of Mechanism — explain how the feature constitutes an instance of the claim limitation; (4) Explicit Contention — explicit assertions rather than vague references like "see, for example."

rubrics_metrics.name: "Aping" the claim language as the common deficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely repeating claim language without explanation constitutes inadequate charting. For example, asserting "Product X includes a framis because it has a framis" adds nothing without explaining what constitutes a "framis" under the proper claim construction and how Product X's component satisfies that definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the clearest single criterion in the source for spotting a "stretch"/weak mapping — the assertion restates the claim term instead of independently establishing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents — function/way/result
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond literal infringement, a limitation may be found present through the Doctrine of Equivalents: a feature that differs from the claim limitation may still satisfy it if it performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result. Claim charts should explicitly identify which limitations are asserted under literal infringement, which under DoE, and the functional-equivalence reasoning supporting DoE assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — single reference discloses every limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A single piece of prior art that discloses every limitation of an asserted claim, exactly as claimed, renders the claim invalid. The analysis mirrors infringement charting: identify each limitation of the claim and demonstrate that a single prior-art reference contains each limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — motivation to combine multiple references
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention would have been obvious to a person skilled in the field at the time of invention, based on the combination of multiple prior-art references or knowledge in the field. This analysis requires: identifying the motivation to combine separate prior-art references; establishing that combining them would have been obvious; demonstrating that the resulting combination renders each claim limitation obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-filing investigation — reverse engineering and public-source exhaustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Before filing an infringement lawsuit, the patent owner must conduct a reasonable investigation into the accused product, based on publicly available information: attempting to acquire and inspect the accused product; reverse engineering (examining externals, disassembling components, analyzing software through decompilation or dynamic analysis); diligently searching for technical documentation, manuals, specifications, and other publicly accessible materials; documenting the investigation to demonstrate "exhaustion" of public sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes the foundation for "plausible" infringement contentions required under pleading standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Patent Rule contention requirements (infringement and invalidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement Contentions (submitted early): a chart for each asserted claim and each accused product; specific identification of where each limitation appears; explanation of how each limitation is satisfied; identification of claim construction relied upon; for means-plus-function limitations, identification of the corresponding structure; for DoE assertions, explanation of functional equivalence. Invalidity Contentions (submitted by defendant): a chart for each asserted claim and each prior-art reference; specific identification of where each limitation appears in the prior art; explanation of how each limitation is disclosed; for obviousness, identification of the motivation to combine multiple references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendment restrictions: once contentions are submitted, amendments require "good cause" — courts examine whether new information was genuinely unavailable despite diligent search, whether the party could have obtained it earlier, and whether the amendment represents a significant shift in theory rather than mere refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worked example: mapping "a web server for transmitting data to client devices"
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim reciting "a web server for transmitting data to client devices": (1) establish claim construction (define "web server" through specification, industry standards, and technical understanding, not merely accept vendor labels); (2) identify location in accused product (e.g., "SERVER.EXE file located in D:\Applications\"); (3) provide supporting facts (e.g., "Product manual Section 3.2 describes how the server transmits data; source code reveals HTTP protocol implementation"); (4) explain the connection ("The identified component implements the HTTP protocol and responds to client requests by transmitting data in standard web formats, thereby satisfying the construction of 'web server.'").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish from mere assertion: avoid stating only "Product X includes a web server" without the explanatory foundation.
